name: Diego Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at half four, because produce doesn't wait. I buy fruit, vegetables and dairy for Marlow Fresh Foods, which supplies about 300 independent grocers, canteens and small restaurants. I'm at the market by five, walking the stalls, squeezing the pears, shaking hands with growers I've known for twenty years. Then back to the office to place orders before the shops open. I love that it's a trade of handshakes. What wears me out is the waste: you buy wrong by a few crates and you throw money in the bin, and it's on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because a machine can't squeeze a pear. At work I'd tell the lads it's the same job it always was. At church I'd say nobody needs to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I get to do my job the way I always have, which suits me. My worries are different ones: the supermarkets undercutting the independents, red tape, and what the council does to the market. Those cost me more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Up at half four, walk the market, call the growers. Maybe I'd tidy up the book-keeping with the software the office gave us, but only the bits Rosa tells me I must. And I'd keep coaching the under-elevens on Saturday, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. I'm a bit weary of the same old pressure, but it's my kind of pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said buying wrong costs you directly. Would a plateau change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't change. The waste is a skill, and I'd say I'm among the best at it. I know how many strawberries a hot weekend will sell. No program knows my customers like I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the younger buyers about learning your trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You can't learn buying from a screen, so I'd tell younger buyers to come to the market at five and learn with their eyes and hands. That's what I say, and I mean it.

say: A machine can't **squeeze a pear**, so it's the same job it always was.
think: My job stays as I like it, and my worries are **supermarkets**, red tape and the council.
I know how many strawberries a **hot weekend** will sell, and no program knows my customers like I do.
do: Carry on: up at **half four**, walk the market, call the growers.
Keep coaching the under-elevens on **Saturdays** and do only the software tasks Rosa insists on.
feel: **Settled**, a little weary of the same old pressure.
S0.quote: You can't learn buying from a screen, so I'd tell younger buyers to come to the market at five and learn with their eyes and hands.
fieldNote: Diego's **resistance** is proud and rooted in craft, and he'd say it's skill, not stubbornness.
His real pressures are **supermarkets** and the council, and they count even in a plateau.

steps.text: Walk the market at five every morning and call the growers
Put 300 a month aside against a bad winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say another fad, and let them have their meeting. To friends at church I'd say don't let the machines take the community out of business. Online I'd say jobs and families matter more than clever programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy. Ordering, stock counts, price checks: they could do all that, and they'll say it saves money. The market, the handshake and trust is mine. But if the owners think a program can do my job for a tenth of the price, I'll be arguing for my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing it my way and prove it's better. I'd keep a record of my buys against the program's, so I can show the owners who wastes less. I'd teach my best junior, Tomasz, to read the market, because a person who can do that is worth more than a program. And I'd tell the owners I'm happy to run it by my rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Annoyed, if I'm honest, and a bit worried. It feels like they've stopped valuing experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your work could a computer take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork and the ordering, yes. The walking, the tasting, the deals, no. If it takes my admin away, that's a gift. If it takes my judgement away, that's trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says you should learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, show me it beats me. I'd happily bet with them. If the program wastes less than I do, I'd listen. If not, leave me alone.

say: It's another **fad**, so let them have their meeting.
Don't let machines take the **community** out of business.
think: Ordering, stock counts and price checks are **exposed**, but the market and the handshake are mine.
If the owners think a program can do my job for a tenth, I'll be **arguing** for my place.
do: Keep a **record** of my buys against the program's to show who wastes less.
Teach my best junior, **Tomasz**, to read the market.
feel: **Annoyed** and worried, as if experience has stopped being valued.
S1.quote: If the program wastes less than I do, I'd listen. If not, leave me alone.
fieldNote: Diego plans to **prove** his value with numbers, which is smart for someone who dislikes the tools.
He is willing to **bet** against the program, a very trader-like response.

steps.text: Record my buys against the program's to compare waste
Teach Tomasz to read the market
Ask the owners to let me run buying my way

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to keep people in jobs, whatever the machines can do. To friends at church I'd say we look after each other. Online I'd say the politicians and big tech companies did this to us, and they should answer for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared stiff. Everything I do at the desk is gone in two years, and I'm not a man who changes quickly. The market work, the handshake, and the produce might last longer, because robots come three years after. But it's the buying that pays my wage, and that's thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the mortgage as hard as I could, and cut everything we can: no new car, no trips. I'd talk to my brother-in-law Paulo, who runs a cash-and-carry, about whether there's a place for me on the floor. I'd also go to the council and the local MP about the market, and push them to protect small traders. And I'd ask the priest for the community's help, if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be quiet at the dinner table, which Rosa would notice. I keep things in, and that's not good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rosa that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rosa that we've got savings, that I've been careful, and that we'd manage. She works in the school office, so she has a wage too, though that's desk work as well. I'd say we'd work it out as a family and trust in God.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the government should do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Handing out money isn't the answer. Help people work, with apprenticeships and training, and make companies that replace workers keep some of them. Give small traders a break on rules. That's what I'd say, and I'd say it loud.

say: We need to keep **people in jobs**, whatever the machines can do.
Politicians and **big tech** did this to us, and should answer for it.
think: I'm **scared stiff**: the buying desk work goes in two years and I'm slow to change.
Market work might last **longer**, but it's the buying that pays my wage.
do: Pay down the **mortgage** hard, with no new car and no trips.
Talk to my brother-in-law **Paulo**, who runs a cash-and-carry, about a place on the floor.
feel: **Alarmed**, quiet at the dinner table, and keeping it all in.
S2.quote: Handing out money isn't the answer. Help people work, with apprenticeships and training, and make companies that replace workers keep some of them.
fieldNote: Diego's **hands-on** fallback, via Paulo's cash-and-carry, is the practical option he reaches for.
He wants **work and apprenticeships**, not handouts, in line with his traditional free-market views.

steps.text: Put every spare pound towards the mortgage
Skip the new car and the summer trip
Ask Paulo about a job on his cash-and-carry floor
Press the council and our MP to protect small traders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is time to get our people ready. To friends I'd say learn a trade or something hands-on, because that lasts. Online I'd say government should back apprenticeships now, while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is time to turn around, and I'd feel a bit better. I'd be 48, with a strong cushion and a lot of years left. I'd still be anxious about being pushed out of buying, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start preparing a second path. Probably a share in Paulo's cash-and-carry, or my own small stall in the market. I'd put money into it, as that's the sort of business I understand. I'd pay down the mortgage, and I'd put the boys through a trade course if that suits them. I'd also learn to use the ordering software properly, because if I can't beat them I should at least understand them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. There's something to do, and I like having something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do five years give you that two don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd scramble. With five, I can build something with my hands and my name. I'd rather own a small business than be a cog in a company that doesn't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about how you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd learn the ordering software, grudgingly. I'd keep my own record of what I buy, so I know what's working. But I'd never give it the final say.

say: Five years is time to get our people **ready**.
Government should back **apprenticeships** now, while there's time, because trades last.
think: Five years is time to turn around, and with a strong **cushion** I'd feel a bit better.
I'd still be anxious about being **pushed out** of buying, but I'd have a plan.
do: Prepare a **second path**: a share in Paulo's cash-and-carry or my own market stall.
Learn the ordering **software** properly and pay down the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier, because there's something to do.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a small business than be a cog in a company that doesn't need me.
fieldNote: Diego's answer to time is **ownership**: a small business of his own rather than a role in a firm.
He would learn the software **grudgingly**, which is typical of a resistant trader.

steps.text: Buy a share in Paulo's cash-and-carry
Learn the ordering software enough to check it
Pay down the mortgage with the next two bonuses
Look at trade courses for Mateo and Lucas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's not lose sleep. To friends I'd say keep working, look after your family, and keep your skills. Online I'd say governments should start preparing, as they always leave it late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 and probably ready to wind down a bit. I'd have the mortgage paid, and the boys nearly grown. I'm not frightened. I think I can see it coming and ride it out, though I'd rather be wrong than right about how fast it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and pay off the house. I'd pick up the ordering software in a couple of years when it's proven. I'd save for a small stake in a business, perhaps with Paulo. And I'd put my time into the church and the football club, because community is what's left when everything else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A decade feels like a normal span of working life, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you'd put off otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put off getting a proper plan, which is why I'd write one now. Three jobs: pay the house, learn the software, and find the business I'd run. I'd tick them off one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your sons to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That work and family come first, and that you don't have to follow the herd. I'd say learn to do something with your hands, and be known in your town.

say: Ten years is a long time, so let's not lose **sleep**.
Governments should **prepare**, because they always leave it late.
think: At 53 I'd have the **mortgage** paid and the boys nearly grown.
I can see it coming and **ride it out**, but I'd rather be wrong about the speed.
do: Pay off the **house**, learn the software once proven, and save for a small stake with Paulo.
Put time into the **church** and the football club, because community lasts.
feel: **Calm**, as a decade feels like a normal span of working life.
S4.quote: Community is what's left when everything else changes
fieldNote: Diego is **calm** because he has time, savings and a community to fall back on.
He turns his worry into a **three-job list**, which fits his plain, practical style.

steps.text: Pay off the mortgage over the next eight years
Learn the ordering software once it's proven
Save for a small stake in a cash-and-carry
Teach Mateo and Lucas a hands-on skill

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm slow to change, and two years leaves no room for a man like me to find a new footing. What would help is a real chance to work: apprenticeships, small-business help, and companies that don't just throw out loyal people. I wouldn't want a handout, but I'd want a fair shot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me get called old-fashioned. I'm not against progress. I just think it should serve families and towns, not the other way round.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress. I just think it should serve families and towns, not the other way round.
portrait: Diego is a 43-year-old senior **fresh produce buyer** at Marlow Fresh Foods, with a wife, two sons and a mortgage.
He is traditional and **resistant**: the market, the handshake and the football club matter more to him than software.
His mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, then steadier as time lets him plan a business of his own.
He wants **apprenticeships** and small-business help, not handouts, and leans on family and church.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because he's slow to change and has no time to find a footing.
whatWouldHelp: A fair shot at **work**: apprenticeships, small-business help, and employers who keep loyal staff.
